background.definition: Brucellosis is a zoonotic infection caused by the bacteria genus Brucella. It has important global public health implications because it is still common in many countries and because of its potential use in biological warfare. It can infect virtually any organ system, most typically involving pulmonary, hepatobiliary, osteoarticular, genitourinary, and neurologic systems.

list.listitem: Approximately 500,000 new cases occur worldwide each year.
Annual incidence in the United Kingdom and most parts of the United States is 0.3 cases per million, but can be as high as 1 case per 1000 in endemic areas.
Cases in the United States are usually seen in Texas, California, Virginia, or Florida.
Brucella has gained renewed interest because of its potential use in biological warfare, stemming from its high rate of infectivity through airborne transmission.
Brucella is a small, Gram-negative aerobic coccobacillus that grows extracellularly and intracellularly within macrophages.
Of the 6 species, only 4 are known to cause infections in humans: Brucella melitensis, Brucella abortus, Brucella suis, and Brucella canis.
The incubation period can last from 1 day to 60 days to many months. Symptoms are nonspecific and do not depend on the route of transmission.

Brucella is transmitted to humans either by direct contact via cuts or abrasions, through inhalation, or by consuming contaminated unpasteurized dairy products. Person-to-person transmission rarely follows blood transfusion, sexual contact, bone marrow transplant, and vertical transmission.
Brucella invades the immune system by protein inhibition of macrophage apoptosis and the secretion of a soluble tumor necrosis factor-α inhibitor.
Brucella targets phagocytes, replicating without affecting cellular viability. And by turning off apoptosis, it renders the cell immortal, thus allowing for its own survival.

list.listitem: Based on retrospective reviews of patients with confirmed brucellosis, the most common presenting symptoms are undulant fever (60%-88%), fatigue (49%-81%), arthralgias (43%-69%), headaches (35%-41%), diaphoresis (27%-59%), weight loss (13%-17%), depression/irritability (14%), and anorexia (12%-43%).

Approximately one-fourth of patients have respiratory symptoms, nearly one-third of patients have gastrointestinal symptoms, approximately one-third have signs of joint inflammation, and one-fourth have hepatosplenomegaly. Fewer than 10% have lymphadenopathy.
Up to 10% of patients with brucellosis develop vertebral osteomyelitis.
Genitourinary manifestations such as epididymo-orchitis and testicular pain and swelling occur in approximately 2% of patients.

In a prospective study of 140 Turkish patients with abnormal Brucella serology, 9 of the patients (~6%) developed nonspecific cutaneous manifestations attributed to brucellosis: nonspecific rash (2), erythema nodosum (2), psoriatic-appearing lesions (1), palmar erythema (1), malar rash (1), and palmar eczema (1).

Numerous case studies report cardiovascular manifestations (such as endocarditis, myocarditis, pericarditis, and aortic aneurysms) and neurobrucellosis (manifesting with depression, fatigue, and central nervous system invasion).

Initial testing should include serologic studies and a culture. Serologic testing includes the Rose Bengal test, serum agglutination test (SAT), ELISA, the Coombs test, and a Brucella IgG/IgM flow assay.

ELISA is somewhat more sensitive than SAT, and less prone to cross-reactions. ELISA can also determine the specific IgA, IgM, and IgA Brucella antibodies in the blood, serum, and CSF. The Rose Bengal test is quick, inexpensive, and can be used for rapid screening in endemic areas.

A presumptive diagnosis of brucellosis is made when a specific antibody response is seen (>1:160 dilution or 4-fold rise between acute and convalescent phase) or if Brucella sp. is identified by immunofluorescence.

Polymerase chain reaction assays allow for the detection of specific Brucella DNA but they are expensive, time consuming, and require special laboratories and trained personnel who are usually not available in endemic areas. Their clinical role is yet to be defined.

Fluorescence polarization assays, capable of use at the point of care without a laboratory, have been validated for the diagnosis of bovine, ovine, and swine brucellosis, but has not been fully tested for humans. These assays show increased sensitivity when combined with ELISA and a cut-off value of 88.5 mp is used.

Definitive diagnosis is made by isolating the organism through culture of serum, tissue, or bone marrow. Though definitive diagnosis is made through culture, blood culture has a reported sensitivity of 40% to 90% and tissue culture may miss up to 70% of cases. Also, the ability to detect Brucella from culture may be reduced by its slow growth and need for extended incubation.

summarizes the approach to managing the patient with suspected brucellosis; summarizes treatment recommendations.
Adults with brucellosis should be treated with 3 drugs: doxycycline for 6 weeks, rifampin for 6 weeks, and gentamicin for 2 weeks. A
Quinolones should not be used as first-line therapy in the treatment of patients with brucellosis. B
Patients with vertebral osteomyelitis should be treated for 3 months. B

In a systematic review of 30 randomized trials with nearly 4000 patients with brucellosis, regimens using 3 drugs were superior to those using 2 drugs; quinolones were less effective than nonquinolones; and regimens with a combination of a tetracycline and an aminoglycoside were more effective than regimens with a tetracycline and rifampin.
The rate of failure in patients treated with tetracyclines plus streptomycin was lower than patients treated with tetracyclines and rifampin (11% vs 15%; NNT = 7; 95% CI, 5-12).

The rate of failure in patients treated without quinolones was lower than in patients treated with regimens including quinolones (12% vs 18%; NNT = 5; 95% CI, 10-64). However, a Cochrane review found no difference in effectiveness of quinolone-based vs non-quinolone regimens.

In 2 randomized trials comparing 3-drug regimens with 2-drug regimens, the risk of failure of 2-drug regimens was double that of the 3-drug regimens (OR = 2.5; 95% CI, 1.26-5.0). The authors do not report the actual rates of failure, however.
Patients with vertebral osteomyelitis should be treated for 3 months.

Although largely unstudied, some patients with complications such as aortic valve endocarditis, spinal cord compression, and abscesses require surgery.

If left untreated, brucellosis may lead to relapse and complications such as arthritis, sacroiliitis, spondylitis, encephalitis, endocarditis, epididymo-orchitis, and abortion. The fatality rate is less than 2% in untreated patients. B

Two-drug regimens have significantly higher failure rates than 3-drug regimens. Pregnant women may be treated with a 3-drug regimen if counseled about potential risk to fetus. Breastfeeding women should stop breastfeeding when possible.
